textTitles: Why the air is getting dustier
Who gets to name a species?

paragraphs.text: Most of what people read in a year was written in another language. Manuals, contracts, labels, subtitles, safety notices and a large share of the news arrive through a process that the reader is not supposed to notice, and the measure of a good translation has always been that nobody thinks about it. The industry that produces this work is larger than publishing and almost entirely invisible, which has consequences for how it is paid and how it is judged.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first thing to understand is that translation is not a search for equivalents. A competent translator reads a sentence, works out what it is doing — informing, warning, persuading, amusing — and writes a sentence in another language that does the same job for a different reader. Word-for-word correspondence is usually the sign of a poor translation rather than a faithful one, and the difficulty rises with everything that a text carries beyond its literal content: jokes, courtesy, register and the assumptions a writer did not think worth stating.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Specialisation runs deeper than the public assumes. A legal translator needs to know how two legal systems differ, because a term may have no counterpart at all and must be rendered by a description; a medical translator works within a vocabulary where a small error is dangerous; a technical translator spends a good part of the day on terminology management rather than on prose. Literary translation, which is what the word usually conjures, is a small fraction of the market and the only part of it that is reviewed in newspapers.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Machines have changed the work without removing it. Statistical systems of the 2000s produced text that was useful for gist and unusable for publication; the systems that replaced them produce fluent output whose errors are harder to spot precisely because the surface is smooth. The result is a new task: reading machine output against the source and repairing it, which is now a large share of paid work in the industry. Whether this is easier than translating from scratch depends on the quality of the raw output, and translators report that a mediocre draft is slower to fix than an empty page.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The economics have moved accordingly, and not in the direction of the people doing the work. Rates for repairing machine output are set below rates for translation, the volumes are larger, and the speed expected is higher; several surveys report falling real incomes for translators in exactly the language pairs where the machines are strongest. The countries and languages where the machines are weakest — those with less text available to train on — have seen the opposite, which is a reversal of the usual pattern in which technology reaches the richest markets first.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Quality is hard to measure and is therefore measured badly. A common industry metric counts errors per thousand words by category, which works for terminology and punctuation and says nothing about whether a text achieves what it was written to achieve. Buyers who use such metrics often end up with translations that score well and read strangely, and the better agencies supplement them with review by a second linguist. The cost of that review is the first thing cut when a budget is squeezed, and it is the part that catches the errors that matter.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The stakes are visible when the work is done badly. Mistranslated dosing instructions have injured patients, a misrendered clause has cost a company a contract, and in international agreements the question of which language version prevails is negotiated as carefully as the substance. Interpreting — the spoken equivalent, done in real time — carries the same risks in courtrooms and hospitals, where an untrained relative is still too often used because a qualified interpreter costs money and takes time to arrange.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the trade asks for is unglamorous. Enough time to read the whole document before starting; access to the author for the two questions that resolve the ambiguities; a glossary agreed in advance; and payment that reflects the responsibility rather than the keystrokes. None of that is expensive compared with the cost of the errors it prevents, and almost none of it appears in the procurement rules under which most translation is bought.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Why the air is getting dustier

paragraphs.text: Dust is the most under-studied part of the atmosphere for a simple reason: it is difficult to weigh. Every year somewhere between one and five billion tonnes of mineral particles are lifted from dry ground into the air, carried for hundreds or thousands of kilometres and dropped again, and the width of that estimate tells you how uncertain the accounting is. The uncertainty matters, because dust does several large and opposite things at once. A substance that cools the planet, feeds an ocean and fills a hospital ward is difficult to be simply for or against.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: It cools and it warms. Light-coloured particles high in the atmosphere reflect sunlight back to space, which cools the surface beneath them; darker particles absorb energy and warm the layer of air they occupy; dust that settles on snow and ice makes the surface darker, so it absorbs more and melts sooner. Which effect dominates depends on the size and colour of the grains and on what lies beneath them, and the models that try to add it all up disagree about the sign of the total in several regions. That is an unusual admission in climate science, where most quantities are at least known to push in one direction.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Dust also feeds things. Iron carried in mineral dust is a limiting nutrient over large areas of ocean, and the phosphorus that reaches the Amazon basin from North African deserts each year is measured in millions of tonnes; the forest depends on a supply that is blown across an ocean. On land, loess soils — some of the most fertile in the world — are accumulated dust, laid down over tens of thousands of years, and the agricultural heartlands of several countries sit on them. Dust, in other words, built the fields that grow the food, over a period no policy can imitate.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The harm is mostly to lungs. Fine mineral particles penetrate deep into the airway, and in regions downwind of large sources the number of days on which air quality standards are exceeded is driven by dust rather than by traffic. Dust also carries what is on the ground with it, including agricultural chemicals and, in some regions, spores of the fungus that causes a serious lung infection, whose incidence rises in the season after dust storms. Exposure is worst for people who work outdoors and for those whose houses are not sealed, which is the usual distribution of environmental harm.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Whether the world is getting dustier is a genuinely open question. Ice cores and lake sediments show that dust rose substantially during the twentieth century, and satellite records since the 1980s show no simple global trend but sharp regional ones, upwards in central Asia and downwards over parts of the Sahara. The disagreement in the literature is not about the measurements but about how much of the change is caused by land use and how much by shifts in wind and rainfall that would have happened anyway.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Human contributions are easiest to see where a water body has gone. Draining a lake for irrigation exposes a bed of fine sediment that had been under water for millennia, and the resulting dust — often salty and sometimes carrying the residues of whatever was used upstream — blows onto the surrounding population. Several of the worst dust sources in the world today were lakes within living memory, and the pattern is being repeated wherever an inland sea is used faster than it is filled.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The measures that work are the ones that keep soil covered. Leaving crop residue on the surface rather than ploughing it in, planting shelter belts across the prevailing wind, and grazing at a density the land can carry all cut emission substantially, and all of them cost the farmer something in the short term. Where a government has paid for the transition rather than legislating for it, adoption has been faster, which is the same finding that appears in almost every branch of soil conservation.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Forecasting has improved faster than prevention. Dust storms can now be predicted several days ahead with enough accuracy to close schools, ground aircraft and warn people with respiratory conditions, and several regional centres issue such warnings routinely. It is a useful capability and an incomplete answer: a forecast tells a city when the dust is coming, and does nothing about the dry lake bed it is coming from.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Who gets to name a species?

paragraphs.text: Naming a species is a formal act with rules older than most scientific institutions. A researcher who believes an organism is new publishes a description, designates a preserved specimen as the permanent reference, and proposes a two-part name; if the description meets the requirements of the relevant code, the name is valid and the person who published it is the author. The system has worked for two and a half centuries and is now the subject of an argument that its rules did not anticipate.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Dr Selina Marr defends the rules as they are. The strength of the system, she argues, is that it is mechanical: priority goes to the first valid publication, the criteria are formal, and no committee decides whether a name is appropriate. Once a name can be challenged on grounds of taste or politics, every name becomes provisional, and a nomenclature whose entries can be revisited is not a stable reference for the millions of records already attached to it. Her position is not that all existing names are admirable, but that stability is the property the system exists to provide.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Professor Daniel Okonkwo puts the case for change. A significant number of species carry names honouring people who were slave traders or colonial administrators, or names derived from insults in local languages, and these are not historical curiosities: they are used today by the people who live where the species lives. He notes that the codes already permit changes in some circumstances and that a mechanism for exceptional cases would not collapse the system, since committees already rule on other kinds of dispute without the sky falling.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Dr Hana Ishii works on a different dimension of the same problem. A large share of the species described in the past two centuries were collected in countries other than the one where they were described, and the type specimen — the permanent reference — usually sits in a museum in the collecting country’s capital rather than in the country of origin. Any researcher in the country where the species lives must travel to examine it, and the cost of that travel has shaped who can work on what. Digitisation helps and is not a substitute for the specimen.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Dr Marcus Vey raises the practical question of who does the naming now. The description of new species has shifted towards countries with strong research funding, and taxonomy itself is poorly funded almost everywhere; the number of working taxonomists in some groups is smaller than it was thirty years ago, while the number of undescribed species is estimated in millions. Whatever is decided about existing names, he argues, the binding constraint is that there are not enough people to describe what is being lost.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Positions have moved on one point. Naming a new species after a living person who paid for the privilege — an established fundraising practice for some institutions — is now widely criticised, including by researchers who defend the stability of older names, on the grounds that it makes the name a commodity. The codes do not forbid it, and several journals have begun to decline such descriptions, which is a change in practice achieved without changing a rule.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Where the codes have been revised, the revisions have been cautious. A recent change allows a small category of names to be set aside, with the decision taken by a committee and applied prospectively rather than retroactively. Supporters describe it as an overdue safety valve; critics point out that the committee is small and that a rule which depends on judgement will be applied unevenly. Both descriptions are accurate, which is the usual situation when a formal system acquires a discretionary element.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The argument matters more than it appears to. A name is the key to everything recorded about an organism — its conservation status, its role in an ecosystem, the laws that protect it — and a name that people refuse to use produces a literature that is hard to search. Whatever is decided, the deciding will be done largely by institutions in a small number of countries, which is itself one of the things being argued about, and is the part least likely to change quickly.
paragraphs.label: H
